parts.title: Vol 12-Section 1
parts.passageHtml:
{[A. Americans today choose among more options in more parts of life than has ever been pos­sible before.][105636]} {[To an extent, the opportunity to choose enhances our lives.][105654]} {[It is only logical to think that if some choices are good, more is better; people who care about having infinite options will benefit from them, and those who do not can always just ignore the 273 versions of cereal they have never tried.][105665]} {[Yet recent research strongly suggests that, psychologically, this assumption is wrong, with 5% lower percentage announcing they are happy.][105710]} {[Although some choices are undoubtedly better than , more is not always better than less.][105730]}

{[B.][105747]} {[Recent research offers insight into why many people end up unhappy rather than pleased when their options expand.][105766]} {[We began by making a distinction between “maximizers” (those who always aim to make the best possible choice) and “satisficers” (those who aim for “good enough,” whether or not better selections might be out there).][105785]}

{[C. In particular, we composed a set of statements—the Maximization Scale—to diagnose peo­ple’s propensity to maximize.][105820]} {[Then we had several thousand people rate themselves from 1 to 7 (from “completely disagree” to “completely agree”) on such statements as “I never settle for second best.][105837]} {[” We also evaluated their sense of satisfaction with their decisions.][105875]} {[We did not define a sharp cutoff to separate maximizers from satisficers, but in general, we think of individuals whose average scores are higher than 4 (the scale’s midpoint) as maxi- misers and those whose scores are lower than the midpoint as satisficers.][105886]} {[People who score highest on the test—the greatest maximizers—engage in more product comparisons than the lowest scorers, both before and after they make purchasing decisions, and they take longer to decide what to buy.][105933]} {[When satisficers find an item that meets their standards, they stop looking.][105970]} {[But maximizers exert enormous effort reading labels, checking out consumer magazines and trying new products.][105982]} {[They also spend more time comparing their purchas­ing decisions with those of others.][105998]}

{[D. We found that the greatest maximizers are the least happy with the fruits of their efforts.][106013]} {[When they compare themselves with others, they get little pleasure from finding out that they did better and substantial dissatisfaction from finding out that they did worse.][106030]} {[They are more prone to experiencing regret after a purchase, and if their acquisition disappoints them, their sense of well-being takes longer to recover.][106058]} {[They also tend to brood or ruminate more than satisficers do.][106082]}

{[E. Does it follow that maximizers are less happy in general than satisficers?][106093]} {[We tested this by having people fill out a variety of questionnaires known to be reliable indicators of well­being.][106106]} {[As might be expected, individuals with high maximization scores experienced less satisfaction with life and were less happy, less optimistic and more depressed than people with low maximization scores.][106125]} {[Indeed, those with extreme maximization ratings had depression scores that placed them on the borderline of clinical range.][106136]}

{[F. Several factors explain why more choice is not always better than less, especially for maxi­misers.][106156]} {[High among these are “opportunity costs.][106172]} {[” The quality of any given option cannot be assessed in isolation from its alternatives.][106179]} {[One of the “costs” of making a selection is losing the opportunities that a different option would have afforded.][106194]} {[Thus, an opportunity cost of vacationing on the beach in Cape Cod might be missing the fabulous restaurants in the Napa Valley.][106212]} {[Early Decision Making Research by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that people respond much more strongly to losses than gains.][106234]} {[If we assume that opportunity costs reduce the overall desirability of the most preferred choice, then the more alternatives there are, the deeper our sense of loss will be and the less satisfaction we will derive from our ultimate decision.][106256]}

{[G. The problem of opportunity costs will be better for a satisficer.][106299]} {[The latter’s “good enough” philosophy can survive thoughts about opportunity costs.][106310]} {[In addition, the “good enough” standard leads to much less searching and inspection of alternatives than the maximizer’s “best” standard.][106323]} {[With fewer choices under consideration, a person will have fewer opportu­nity costs to subtract.][106345]}

{[H. Just as people feel sorrow about the opportunities they have forgone, they may also suffer regret about the option they settled on.][106360]} {[My colleagues and I devised a scale to measure proneness to feeling regret, and we found that people with high sensitivity to regret are less happy, less satisfied with life, less optimistic and more depressed than those with low sensitivity.][106383]} {[Not surprisingly, we also found that people with high regret sensitivity tend to be maximizers.][106423]} {[Indeed, we think that worry over future regret is a major reason that individuals become maximizers.][106439]} {[The only way to be sure you will not regret a decision is by making the best possible one.][106455]} {[Unfortunately, the more options you have and the more opportunity costs you incur, the more likely you are to experience regret.][106474]} {[I.][106496]} {[In a classic demonstration of the power of sunk costs, people were offered season subscrip­tions to a local theatre company.][106515]} {[Some were offered the tickets at full price and others at a discount.][106534]} {[Then the researchers simply kept track of how often the ticket purchasers actu­ally attended the plays over the course of the season.][106547]} {[Full-price payers were more likely to show up at performances than discount payers.][106569]} {[The reason for this, the investigators argued, was that the full-price payers would experience more regret if they did not use the tickets because not using the more costly tickets would constitute a bigger loss.][106584]} {[To increase a sense of happiness, we can decide to restrict our options when the decision is not crucial.][106620]} {[For example, make a rule to visit no more than two stores when shopping for clothing.][106639]}

{[H. Just as people feel sorrow about the opportunities they have forgone, they may also suffer regret about the option they settled on.][106656]} {[My colleagues and I devised a scale to measure proneness to feeling regret, and we found that people with high sensitivity to regret are less happy, less satisfied with life, less optimistic and more depressed than those with low sensitivity.][106679]} {[Not surprisingly, we also found that people with high regret sensitivity tend to be maximizers.][106719]} {[Indeed, we think that worry over future regret is a major reason that individuals become maximizers.][106735]} {[The only way to be sure you will not regret a decision is by making the best possible one.][106751]} {[Unfortunately, the more options you have and the more opportunity costs you incur, the more likely you are to experience regret.][106770]}

{[I.][106793]} {[In a classic demonstration of the power of sunk costs, people were offered season subscrip­tions to a local theatre company.][106803]} {[Some were offered the tickets at full price and others at a discount.][106822]} {[Then the researchers simply kept track of how often the ticket purchasers actu­ally attended the plays over the course of the season.][106835]} {[Full-price payers were more likely to show up at performances than discount payers.][106857]} {[The reason for this, the investigators argued, was that the full-price payers would experience more regret if they did not use the tickets because not using the more costly tickets would constitute a bigger loss.][106871]} {[To increase a sense of happiness, we can decide to restrict our options when the decision is not crucial.][106904]} {[For example, make a rule to visit no more than two stores when shopping for clothing.][106923]}

questionSets.instructionHtml:
Questions 1 - 4:

Look at the following descriptions or deeds (Questions 1-4) and the list of catego­ries below. Match each description or deed with the correct category, A-D.

Write the correct letter, A-D, in boxes 1-4 on your answer sheet.

A          “maximizers”
B          “satisficers”
C          neither “maximizers” nor “satisficers”
D          both “maximizers” and “satisficers”
questionSets.contentHtml:
Rated to the Maximization Scale of making choice 1

Don’t take much time before making a decision 2

Are likely to regret about the choice in the future 3

Choose the highest price in the range of purchase 4

questions.explanationHtml:
D
Đọc kĩ nghiên cứu khảo sát ở đoạn C. Nghiên cứu này nhằm chẩn đoán xu hướng tối ưu hoá của con người. Người ta sẽ đánh giá vài người trên thang điểm từ 1 - 7 theo thang "Maximization Scale". Những người này sẽ đồng ý hoặc không đồng ý với những câu kiểu như "Tôi chưa bao giờ chấp nhận lựa chọn tốt nhì". Những người trên 4 điểm là "maiximisers" - người tối ưu hoá, luôn đi so sánh sản phẩm, luôn muốn chọn ra sản phẩm tốt nhất nên khi mua thường tốn nhiền thời gian hơn. Những người dưới 4 điểm là "satisficers" - người hài lòng, khi sản phẩm đáp ứng được nhu cầu của họ thì họ sẽ ngừng việc tìm kiếm
Cả 2 nhóm người "maximisers" và "satisficers" đều được đo lường dựa vào thang "Maximization Scale" - "Thang đo tối ưu hoá lựa chọn"

questionSets.instructionHtml:
Questions 5 - 8:

Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 5-8 on your answer sheet, write

TRUE                 if the statement is true

FALSE                if the statement is false

NOT GIVEN      if the information is not given in the passage

questions.text: In today’s world, since the society is becoming wealthier, people are happier.
questions.explanationHtml:
FALSE
 
Ngày này cuộc sống phát triển hơn, giàu có hơn khi con người có nhiều cơ hội để lựa chọn hơn, nhưng điều đó không có nghĩa họ hạnh phúc hơn. Số liệu nghiên cứu chỉ ra rằng, khi có nhiều cơ hội hơn, chỉ dưới 5% số người nói rằng họ hạnh phúc, đa số đều không hạnh phúc

questions.text: In society, there are more maximisers than satisficers.
questions.explanationHtml:
NOT GIVEN
 
"In society, there are more maximisers than satisficers." --> Trong xã hội ngày nay có nhiều "maximisers" hơn "satisficers" là NOT GIVEN vì toàn bài không hề đưa ra thông tin hay số liệu nói về SỐ LƯỢNG "maximisers" hay "satisficers".

questions.text: People tend to react more to loses than gains.
questions.explanationHtml:
TRUE
 
respond much more strongly = react more
Con người phản ứng dữ dội hơn với sự mất mát hơn là sự đạt được điều gì đó

questions.text: Females and males acted differently in the study of choice making.
questions.explanationHtml:
NOT GIVEN
 
Thông tin trong bài không đề cập đến việc giới tính có liên quan đến sự lựa chọn

questionSets.instructionHtml:
Questions 9 - 13:

Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 9-13 on your answer sheet.

options.text: know the happiness when they have more choices.
measure how people are likely to feel after making choices.

questions.explanationHtml:
B
 
Câu B đúng vì thang đo này cho thấy được con người cảm thấy như thế nào sau khi đưa ra sự lựa chọn, phân họ thành 2 nhóm người "maximisers" và "satisficers". Nhóm người "maximisers" thường cảm thấy ít hạnh phúc hơn nhóm "satisficers".
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Câu A sai vì khi có nhiều sự lựa chọn hơn con người không cảm thấy hạnh phúc hơn
Câu C là not given vì thông tin này không có đề cập trong bài
Câu D: giúp người ta giảm thời gian mua hàng là not given vì thông tin này không đề cập trong bài

options.text: People can make choices more easily
Maximizers are happier to make choices.
Satisficers are quicker to make wise choices.
People have more tendency to experience regret.

questions.explanationHtml:
D
 
Đọc thêm giải thích câu 3. Khi người ta có nhiều sự lựa chọn hơn, cũng như khi họ là "maximisers", luôn tìm kiếm sự lựa chọn tốt nhất trong rất rất nhiều sự lựa chọn, họ sẽ trải nghiệm "less satisfaction" - ít sự thoả mãn hơn, ít hạnh phúc hơn và có xu hướng cảm thấy hối hận nhiều hơn.

options.text: they prefer to use more money when buying tickets.
they don’t like to spend more money on theatre.
higher-priced things would induce more regret if not used properly.
full-price payers are real theatre lovers.

questions.explanationHtml:
C
sunk cost: chi phí "chìm" là chi phí đã mất đi và không thể thay đổi được nhưng lại có ảnh hưởng rất lớn đến quyết định của con người
Thí nghiệm trong đoạn I nhằm thể hiện sức mạnh của chi phí "chìm". Các đối tượng trong thí nghiệm này sẽ mua vé xem phim full giá hoặc được giảm giá. Kết quả là nhóm mua full giá đi xem phim thường xuyên hơn nhóm được giảm giá vì họ cảm thấy rằng nếu họ không đi xem phim thì họ sẽ mất đi 1 điều gì đó rất lớn. Tuy nhiên, việc họ đã mua vé xem phim là xảy ra trong quá khứ rồi, là chi phí đã bỏ ra không thể lấy lại rồi, nên việc có xem hay không chẳng ảnh hưởng gì đến cuộc đời họ cả, nhưng vì nuối tiếc, vì chi phí chìm lớn nên họ buộc phải đi xem phim. Nên là những thứ đắt đỏ sẽ mang lại "regret" - hối hận, nuối tiếc rất lớn nếu không được sử dụng đúng đắn

options.text: limit the number of choices in certain situations

questions.explanationHtml:
D
 
restrict = limit: giới hạn
Vậy để tăng cảm giác hạnh phúc thì ta nên giới hạn lại các sự lựa chọn - "options". Ví dụ khi mua quần áo, cố gắng có quy tắc là không đi quá 2 tiệm để lựa
